clue.text: One walking with philosopher goes round a long way

indicators.note: the philosopher's name encircles the distance phrase, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: A. J. Ayer was a British philosopher
a long way off is far

explanation.surface: A rambler and a thinker set off on a lengthy detour together.
explanation.walkthrough: A. J. Ayer is the crossword's go-to philosopher; 'goes round' means his name surrounds the distance word.
explanation.definitionFit: A traveller on foot, especially one making a journey, is a straightforward synonym for someone walking.

clue.text: Prepare oneself to be introduced to big names, worrying unnecessarily

indicators.note: the preparing verb is placed inside the celebrity list

parts.note: the A-list is a set of top celebrities
to arm is to prepare for conflict

explanation.surface: A nervous fan steels themselves before meeting celebrities, fretting needlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be introduced to' means the arming verb is slipped inside the list of celebrities, which is written without its hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarmist person spreads or feels needless fear, exaggerating dangers.

clue.text: Fish finds no width to glide beneath

indicators.note: the width letter is absent from the gliding word

parts.note: to flow is to glide smoothly along
under means beneath

explanation.surface: A fish loses its streamlined shape and can only slide along the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no width' takes W out of FLOW, giving FLO.
explanation.definitionFit: The flounder is a flatfish found in coastal waters.

clue.text: Show astonishment as insurgent loses heart

indicators.note: the central letter of the word is removed

parts.note: an insurgent is a rebel

explanation.surface: People are amazed as a rebel fighter loses courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses heart' takes B, the middle letter, from REBEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel is to stagger back, as one does when shocked or amazed.

clue.text: Call on miserable chap for currency

parts.note: to ring is to call on the telephone
git is British slang for an unpleasant man

explanation.surface: Someone phones a grumpy man to borrow money.
explanation.walkthrough: GIT is a mild British insult for a contemptible man.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringgit is the monetary unit of Malaysia.

clue.text: Out of trouble, as telephone once unable to ring?

definitions.text: as telephone once unable to ring?
definitions.meaning: an old handset left off its cradle gave an engaged signal, so incoming calls could not get through

explanation.surface: Escaping trouble, like a phone taken off its rest so nobody can call.
explanation.definitionFit: Being let off means escaping punishment or obligation, the idiom's everyday sense.

clue.text: Swiftly bar old stretch of prison

parts.note: an inn is a pub, a bar
time is slang for a prison sentence, as in doing time

explanation.surface: A short prison spell served quickly in a former pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stretch' and 'time' both mean a prison sentence in slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means very quickly or almost at once, an idiom for speed.

clue.text: Busy men argued stupidly university was superfluous

indicators.note: acting stupidly suggests the letters are jumbled foolishly

explanation.surface: Busy men bickered foolishly, though the university was not needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupidly' scrambles MEN ARGUED, and 'was superfluous' means U is a leftover not used. 'Busy' is old British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A French armed police officer is a gendarme, and busy is old British slang for a policeman.

clue.text: Break an item of jewellery into fine pieces

indicators.note: the jewellery goes into the shuffled letters, sitting inside them
broken into pieces, so the letters of fine are smashed up and rebuilt

parts.note: a ring is a piece of jewellery worn on the finger

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a piece of jewellery into tiny fragments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine pieces' reads as tiny fragments, but 'pieces' is the anagram signal and 'into' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To break a rule or law is to transgress against it, the verb's usual sense.

clue.text: Emperor penguin's end, after refusal to cross a part of Antarctica

indicators.note: the penguin's last letter is placed after everything else
the refusal straddles the polar piece, its letters on either side

parts.note: a refusal is a no
the South Pole lies in Antarctica

indicators.note: the end of the word penguin is its final letter

explanation.surface: An emperor penguin meets its end trekking across the frozen south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emperor penguin' reads as the bird, but 'Emperor' alone is the definition. 'to cross' wraps the refusal round the pole; 'end' and 'after' put the penguin's last letter at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804.

clue.text: Go bust after end of scandal makes a big page

indicators.note: the collapse word is placed after the scandal suffix

parts.note: -gate is the suffix ending scandal names like Watergate
a business that goes bust folds

explanation.surface: A newspaper collapses after a scandal and splashes it across a huge page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of scandal' looks like a final letter, but it is the suffix -GATE that ends names of scandals.
explanation.definitionFit: A gatefold is an oversized folded sheet in a magazine or book that opens out wider than normal pages.

clue.text: Very suggestive, dropping article that's malicious

indicators.note: the indefinite article falls out of the longer word

parts.note: indicative means suggestive or pointing to something
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A remark so heavily insinuating that it turns spiteful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' tells you the article falls out of the word for suggestive; 'Very' supplies the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vindictive describes someone set on revenge and wanting to hurt, close in sense to spiteful and malicious.

clue.text: Withdrawal from unfriendly land

parts.note: a cold manner is unfriendly
Turkey is a country

explanation.surface: A retreat from a hostile country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawal' suggests a military pullout, but it means coming off drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for abrupt drug withdrawal and its unpleasant symptoms.

clue.text: Something in the sky —- rook? -—- that goes out over the sea

definitions.text: that goes out over the sea

parts.note: the idiom pie in the sky means an unrealistic hope
R is the chess notation for a rook

explanation.surface: Something spotted overhead — perhaps a rook — flying out to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something in the sky' suggests a bird or cloud; it is the PIE of the phrase 'pie in the sky'.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside pier is a walkway built on stilts that extends from the shore over the water.

clue.text: The way to cause annoyance, staying obstinate to the end like a mule

indicators.note: the final letter stays lodged within the other pieces

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
to rile is to annoy

indicators.note: only the final letter of obstinate is wanted

explanation.surface: A stubborn mule digs in its heels, maddeningly blocking the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like a mule' is fair because mules are hybrids that cannot breed. 'to the end' takes the last letter of obstinate, and 'staying' lodges it between the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Mules, as hybrids of horse and donkey, are almost always infertile and cannot breed.

clue.text: To staff, police officer is a comic figure

parts.note: a super is a superintendent in the police
to man a post is to staff it

explanation.surface: A senior police officer manning the desk turns out to be a figure of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic figure' suggests a clown, but means a hero of comic books.
explanation.definitionFit: The caped hero first appeared in American comic books in 1938.

clue.text: No problem team resolved for a mark

parts.note: something easy is no problem

indicators.note: resolved, in the sense of broken down and settled anew, rearranges the letters of team

explanation.surface: A team easily settles who to target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' rearranges TEAM to MEAT; a 'mark' is a con man's victim.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark is a gullible target for swindlers, someone easily exploited or beaten.

clue.text: Struggle to be capable when books are finally taken away

indicators.note: the books are removed from the very end of the word

parts.note: competent means capable
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to cope once their reference books are removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are finally taken away' strips NT from the end of COMPETENT.
explanation.definitionFit: To compete is to strive or vie against rivals, which is to struggle with them.

clue.text: Given energetic assistance to bury daughter in ground

indicators.note: the daughter is buried within the other word

parts.note: powered means driven by energy, given a boost

explanation.surface: Someone is helped to bury their daughter in the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like soil in the surface; it is a past participle meaning crushed fine.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ground has been crushed to fine particles, i.e. reduced to dust.

clue.text: Brief moment for a visit, being idle

parts.note: a tick is a moment, as in just a tick
over as in coming over to someone's house

explanation.surface: A quick drop-in when someone has nothing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: TICK is British for a short moment.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine that ticks over runs slowly while disengaged, idling, and by extension a thing ticking over is merely ticking along.

clue.text: End up almost poor, with unhealthy air

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the goal word is written bottom to top

parts.note: an aim is an end or goal

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: small, as in a poor or small turnout

explanation.surface: Someone ends up nearly destitute and breathing foul air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns AIM into MIA; 'almost' trims SMALL to SMAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A miasma is a noxious vapour once blamed for disease, so miasmal describes pestilent air.

clue.text: Go by plane, not road, idiot!

indicators.note: the road word is missing from the aircraft word

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: An exasperated traveller shouts that one should fly, not drive, you fool!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go by plane' looks like one phrase about flying; 'Go by' is the definition and 'not road' takes LANE from plane, leaving P.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass something is to go by it, overtaking or moving beyond.

clue.text: Reason and calculate, say, then change mind

definitions.meaning: reason and calculate are two ways to think, so the verb occurs a second time
to reconsider before acting, possibly deciding differently

explanation.surface: A careful person weighs things up, does the sums, and then reverses a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is playful: two verbs that each mean think give the idea of thinking two times.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to reconsider a plan, often leading one to abandon or alter it.

clue.text: Perhaps horns and hoofs used in defence

parts.note: horns belong to a male sheep, which suggests the animal's name
hoofs, like horns, are body parts of that animal, perhaps as the clue says

explanation.surface: An animal's horns and hoofs are its weapons for fighting off attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps horns and hoofs' are examples of RAM PARTS, the bits of a male sheep; read as one word, they are fortifications.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramparts are defensive walls or earth banks surrounding a fort or town.

clue.text: Cover is to get bent, twisted in the middle

indicators.note: only the central pair of letters is turned around

parts.note: to warp is to become bent out of shape

explanation.surface: A sheet gets crumpled and twisted at its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisted in the middle' swaps the A and R at the heart of WARP.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap something is to cover or enfold it in material.

clue.text: More than count as a tomb-robber?

definitions.meaning: a German noble title ranking above a count
jokingly, one who mars or damages a burial site

explanation.surface: A grave-robbing nobleman, worse than any mere count.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the title into MAR GRAVE: a robber who spoils a tomb. The question mark flags this whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: A margrave was a German nobleman, historically a border lord, ranking above an ordinary count.

clue.text: Stories told by our enemies, a hateful thing

parts.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings
them, as in us and them, the opposing side

explanation.surface: Tales spread by the opposition about something detestable.
explanation.walkthrough: ANA, a crossword favourite, is a collection of stories about a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is something intensely loathed, originally a thing cursed by the church.

clue.text: A rapidly turned out sort of inscription

indicators.note: turned out suggests the letters are produced in a new form, rearranged

explanation.surface: An engraver churns out a quick inscription.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' rearranges A RAPIDLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapidary describes something engraved on stone, so a lapidary inscription is a monumental carved one.
